sm: Yaron Brook welcomes Onkar Ghate to discuss Tuesday's midterm elections. Ghate says his reaction was muted: the Republicans deserved to lose big, but the Democrats did not deserve to win, so the result is a vote against something rather than for anything. Both are doubtful the Republicans will learn the right lessons, though Ghate says a landslide loss leaves more room for a candidate not tied to Trump, perhaps someone like Paul Ryan or Adam Kinzinger. Brook mentions Nick Fuentes claiming the party's future belongs to his wing. Ghate warns that young, irrational staffers are gaining influence in party machinery, citing the shift at the Heritage Foundation.

Ghate says it is easy to dismiss these rising factions, just as people dismissed Trump's chances in the last primary, and the old guard has less gatekeeping power than it thinks. The two discuss how voters may face bad choices on both sides, and say the more principled side, however irrational, tends to win in the end. Ghate imagines a reasonable, competent candidate in the mold of Ben Shapiro attracting people tired of irrational extremes, though getting through primaries is the challenge. They say Biden ran only as old and stable, and that voting for Trump empowers the Bernie Sanders wing of the Democratic party.

They turn to the Democratic party, where several far-left candidates won House races. Ghate thinks this reflects the young base and notes that campus life is a sheltered, government-supported environment that people leave when they enter the real world. He finds it ironic that commentators who tolerated Trump's aggressive rhetoric now object to it from the left. Brook is surprised that Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan despite an anti-Israel campaign. Ghate adds that the mixed economy turns old against young, since the welfare state and housing restrictions favor older people, and young people are gravitating toward younger candidates.

The conversation continues on old versus young. They say the age of politicians, with senators dying in office, fuels fatigue, and that corruption ranked even above cost of living in some exit polls. Brook says European young people face a state that spends mostly on redistribution to the old, and Ghate says he is now less sympathetic to protecting current Social Security and Medicare recipients, since the young never had a vote on it. They note French resistance to raising the retirement age. Brook observes that young people are on average doing fine economically, and attributes their pessimism to a lack of values and spiritual emptiness.

Ghate says higher education used to demand more of students, who paid their own way, whereas now government loans and handouts make young people more resentful of work. Brook adds that many believe AI will save them from work. They then discuss Trump's weekend comments that he was perhaps too harsh on immigration and might deal on long-working illegal immigrants. Ghate says Trump is not anti-immigrant and mostly wants prestige rather than power, and Brook notes the comments came right after Stephen Miller was named chief of staff, which Ghate reads as a loyalist choice. Ghate finds the absence of serious economic proposals on inflation depressing.

Brook recalls that deregulation in the 1970s was bipartisan, whereas today nobody proposes anything comparable. Ghate says at least the 1980s discussed money supply and printing money, while today there is no voice like Milton Friedman and little understanding of inflation. Brook says Trump drove out better people like Paul Ryan and Mitt Romney, leaving the least informed and most tribalist, though they might return. They then take audience questions. One person recalls knowing Paul Ryan, and the hosts say he spoke well but voted badly, yet was far better than what exists now. On whether voting for the lesser evil is moral equivocation, Ghate says it depends on context and Ayn Rand set limits on it.

Ghate says that in a free election a vote is a sanction, and Trump treats his vote totals as a mandate, so a vote is for something, not merely against the other side. Both say they have not voted in several elections for that reason. Asked what Objectivists should take from the election, Ghate says there is more to life than politics, but politics matters, since it takes things out of your control, and Brook says to speak up. They joke about a blue wave versus an objective one, saying people must first be educated. Ghate notes the new Texas governor opposes school vouchers.

Brook suggests immigration in Hispanic border counties and anger among Republican women over abortion played a role in Texas, and says Ghate's point that abortion rules mostly hit the young fits the old versus young theme. Both say terrorists played a role in the northern border state of Michigan, which Trump and Vance avoid mentioning. They agree Ayn Rand's influence helped shift the 1970s and 1980s toward respect for business and entrepreneurship, though 9/11 and the financial crisis hurt that attitude, seen now in suspicion of data centers and AI. Ghate thinks Democratic chances in 2028 have fallen since they now hold Congress and must offer a positive vision.

Brook says the Democrats have a stronger bench of centrist figures, such as Ossoff, Cooper and Shapiro, while the Republicans have the same faces, like Rubio, Cruz and DeSantis. They say the Democratic house majority is large, but its socialist wing is energized and will pull the party left. On data centers, they expect more restrictions but think fear of China, national security and AI's share of economic growth will mean slowing rather than ending the industry. They expect Fuentes's wing to grow stronger, and Ghate doubts Vance and Rubio will steer the Republicans off Trump's course. Both find the left and right turning against Israel frightening. On deregulation efforts in New York, Brook calls Mamdani's grocery stores a joke.

Ghate says Mamdani must promote growth, and that the word big is now used as an insult, from the socialist playbook of attacking big corporations. They laugh about criticism of their accents and pronunciation. Brook rejects the idea that hateful movements cannot sustain power, citing the Soviet Union, Nazis and Mao, and says religion's rise among intellectuals worries him. Both say a Putin-like drift toward executive authority is more likely than a dark age. Ghate then answers a question about the word objective, saying that in Objectivism objectivity is a method of knowing reality that involves one's consciousness.

Ghate explains an anti-concept as an illegitimate concept that damages thinking, like a screwdriver that strips the screw. His example is isolationism, which lumped together those opposing US entry into world wars with those who would ignore the world. Brook says similar framing is used about the Iran war. Asked what they would do with billions, Ghate says he would spend it on education, including civics and economics, if effective teachers exist. Brook says he would run for president in 2028, aimed at young people, even knowing he would lose in a landslide, and Ghate notes the audience reaction to Ross Perot's serious style.

Brook recalls Perot treating voters like adults, with graphs about real problems. He and Ghate then answer a question on the Munchausen trilemma. Ghate says Objectivism holds, following Aristotle, that axioms are self-evident starting points known by awareness of reality, which one even uses when denying them, and which need no justification. On what drove the midterm result, they say exit polls suggest a mixture including the Iran war, tariffs and ICE, and that Vance emphasizes only Iran. They think Trump cares about the loss because it is a repudiation, though prestige matters more to him than money. Ghate says he probably would not vote for Ben Shapiro or Mark Levin, since both backed Trump.

Ghate says anyone supporting Trump has a problem, especially given Trump's role in the rise of antisemitism, and Brook adds that a Heritage board addition shows nationalism overriding self-interest. Asked who could propose a new major virtue, Ghate says anyone can propose one in philosophy, but it takes real argument and an exceptionally powerful intellect, and Ayn Rand said Objectivism is her philosophy, so additions are not made by committee. On whether Trump made the Democratic Socialists, Ghate says he made their rise easier by normalizing demonizing groups, though universities also teach socialism. Both say ideas move history only by getting into people's minds and culture. Brook closes the show and says he will return later that day.
